a: Good evening, students. This is a brief update from the main library about the late-night study area on the third floor. Beginning this coming Monday,
the third floor will remain open until two a.m. on weeknights and until midnight on weekends

, so please plan your visits accordingly. A valid university ID is required for entry after eleven p.m., and security staff will check IDs at the elevator lobby. Group study rooms on the third floor can be reserved through the library website, with a maximum of two hours per session. Please remember that food is not allowed in the reading rooms, but covered drinks are welcome. Noise should be kept to a minimum after ten p.m. to respect other students who are preparing for exams. If you need assistance during the extended hours, a reference librarian will be on duty at the front desk until one a.m. on weeknights. Thank you for your cooperation, and good luck with your studies.

Hello everyone, this is a quick message from dining services. During the upcoming reading week, the central dining hall will adjust its schedule. The dining hall will open at ten a.m. and close at eight p.m. from Monday through Friday, and
it will be closed on Saturday for routine maintenance

. Brunch service on Sunday will run from eleven a.m. to two p.m., followed by regular dinner service from five p.m. to nine p.m. Please note that meal plan swipes are accepted during all operating hours, and Flex Dollars can be used at any self-serve station. Students with specific dietary needs are encouraged to speak with a staff member at the welcome counter. For the latest updates, check the dining services page on the student portal. Thank you, and enjoy your reading week.
Attention students and staff. Transportation services is announcing a temporary change to the West Campus shuttle route. Starting tomorrow,
the shuttle will no longer stop at the engineering building due to ongoing construction

. Instead, it will follow a detour through the science plaza and will add a new stop near the recreation center. The revised schedule will keep the same departure times from the main station, with service running every fifteen minutes from seven a.m. to ten p.m. on weekdays. Weekend service will continue every thirty minutes. Riders can find updated route maps posted at each shuttle stop and on the transportation website. We expect the engineering building stop to reopen in about six weeks. Thank you for your patience while we work to keep your travel around campus safe and reliable.
Good afternoon. The student theatre box office is sharing an important update about ticket policies. Beginning next week,
all student ticket prices for mainstage productions will be five dollars, regardless of seat location

. Tickets can be purchased online through the theatre website or in person one hour before each performance. Please bring a valid student ID, as you may be asked to show it at the door. Late seating is not permitted once the performance has begun, so plan to arrive at least ten minutes early. Group discounts are available for parties of ten or more when booked at least three days in advance. Exchanges are allowed up to twenty-four hours before showtime. For questions, contact the box office by email or stop by during regular hours. We look forward to seeing you at the theatre.

Hello, this is a reminder from the career center. Our fall networking night will take place next Thursday from six p.m. to eight p.m. in the student union ballroom. More than forty employers from industries such as finance, engineering, education, and nonprofit work are expected to attend. Students are encouraged to dress in business casual attire and to bring several copies of their resumes. A resume review station will be open from five p.m. to five forty-five p.m. before the event begins. Light refreshments will be provided, and there is no cost to attend. To make the most of the evening, review the list of participating employers on our website and prepare a short self-introduction.
Register online in advance to receive a name tag and a printed directory of employers
. We hope to see you there.

Good morning, students. The student health center is hosting a free flu shot clinic next week. Vaccinations will be available from Monday through Wednesday, between nine a.m. and four p.m., in clinic room B on the second floor. No appointment is necessary, but
please bring your student ID and a completed consent form, which can be downloaded from the health center website

. Students with allergies to eggs or previous vaccine reactions should consult a nurse before receiving the shot. After the injection, you will be asked to wait fifteen minutes in the observation area to make sure you feel well before leaving. The clinic is open to all currently enrolled students and is free of charge while supplies last. For more information, call the health center or visit our page on the student portal. Stay healthy, everyone.
t: Today we are going to look at how mineral deposits form inside limestone caves, and why the process is so sensitive to small changes in water chemistry. Caves develop in regions where rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide as it moves through soil, forming a weak carbonic acid solution. When that slightly acidic water seeps into fractured limestone, it slowly dissolves the rock and enlarges the original cracks into passages. Once a cavity becomes open to air, the chemistry reverses.
Carbon dioxide escapes from the thin film of water clinging to the ceiling, the pH rises, and dissolved calcium carbonate can no longer remain in solution.

The mineral then precipitates around the drip point, building a hollow tube called a soda straw. As the tube grows longer, water may begin to flow along its outside instead, depositing successive rings of calcite that widen the structure into a stalactite. Droplets that fall to the floor lose additional carbon dioxide on impact and deposit calcite upward, forming stalagmites. The shape of every speleothem reflects the balance between drip rate, mineral concentration, and carbon dioxide loss, which is why no two formations look exactly alike.
In this session, I want to consider why animal signals are rarely simple.

A signal has to do two jobs at once. It must travel effectively to the intended receiver, and it must be difficult or costly for predators and competitors to exploit. Natural selection therefore pulls signals in opposite directions.

A brightly coloured bird, for instance, may attract mates more quickly, but the same plumage makes the individual easier for a hawk to detect. That kind of evolutionary tension is called a signaling tradeoff. Many species resolve it by limiting conspicuous displays to brief windows, such as the first minutes of dawn, when low light reduces visibility to predators but still allows conspecifics to read the signal. Other species shift the signaling channel altogether. Some deep-sea fish, for example, produce brief bioluminescent flashes whose colour peaks at wavelengths that penetrate water efficiently and are difficult for many predators to perceive. Across taxa, the recurring pattern is the same: the design of a signal is shaped less by what would be ideal for the receiver than by what competing audiences can and cannot detect.

Let us turn now to the early laboratory work on forgetting, and to a few results that any student of memory should recognise. When Hermann Ebbinghaus tested himself on nonsense syllables at increasing time intervals, he observed a steep initial drop in savings followed by a much slower decline. The pattern, when plotted, resembles a curve that falls sharply and then levels off. Modern replications with broader word lists confirm the qualitative shape, though the absolute rate of loss depends on the material, the retention interval, and the degree of prior learning. The curve has two implications worth noting.

First, the bulk of forgetting happens shortly after learning, so review within the first day yields large gains. Second, because the curve flattens, the marginal benefit of additional review sessions grows smaller over time.

Psychologists therefore recommend a spacing pattern known as expanded rehearsal, in which practice intervals gradually lengthen as the material becomes more stable. The forgetting curve is descriptive, not explanatory. It does not, by itself, tell us whether traces decay, are overwritten, or simply become harder to retrieve. Those are separate theoretical questions.

Our topic this hour is how engineers design buildings to resist earthquake damage, and why flexibility, not raw strength, is the key concept. In a strong tremor, a rigid structure experiences large inertial forces at its base, and brittle materials such as unreinforced masonry crack almost immediately.

Engineers therefore try to lengthen the natural period of the building, which is the time it takes to sway back and forth once, so that the structure does not resonate with the dominant frequencies of the ground motion.

Several strategies are common. Base isolators, often layers of rubber and steel, decouple the building from its foundation and let the ground slide while the structure above moves only slightly. In high-rise construction, a tuned mass damper, essentially a heavy pendulum mounted near the top, can be set in motion opposite to the building's sway, absorbing vibrational energy. Shear walls and moment-resisting frames distribute lateral loads through the floors rather than concentrating stress at any one column. These approaches are complementary. The most resistant buildings combine isolation at the base, a continuous load path through the frame, and damping devices that absorb the energy that isolation alone cannot remove.
Mangrove forests occupy a narrow band along tropical and subtropical coastlines, yet their ecological influence is much wider than their footprint suggests.

The trees are adapted to salt water through specialised root systems that exclude most of the salt at uptake, and through pores in the leaves that excrete the excess. Below the canopy, the architecture of prop and aerial roots slows incoming tides, so waves reaching the interior of the forest carry far less energy than waves at the seaward edge. That buffering effect is one reason coastal communities value mangroves as natural barriers against storm surge. The root matrix also traps fine sediment, allowing the land surface to keep pace with sea level rise in some regions. Biologically, mangrove channels serve as nurseries for juvenile fish, crabs, and mollusks, because the shaded water offers refuge from predators and the leaf litter supports a rich detrital food web. When mangroves are removed, the loss is rarely local. Coastal erosion can accelerate, fisheries decline, and the carbon stored in waterlogged peat can oxidise and enter the atmosphere.

Let us examine the idea of cognitive load, which is central to contemporary instructional design. Working memory holds the information we are actively processing, and it is severely limited in both capacity and duration. Any instructional material that overloads working memory interferes with the construction of stable knowledge in long-term memory. Cognitive load theory distinguishes three sources of demand. Intrinsic load is set by the inherent complexity of the material and the learner's prior knowledge. Extraneous load is imposed by the way the material is presented, for example, by redundant text overlaid on a diagram. Germane load refers to the effort a learner devotes to building mental schemas, which is productive when not crowded out by the other two.
Effective design reduces extraneous load without diluting intrinsic load.

Common strategies include splitting complex procedures into worked examples, aligning narration with on-screen animation, and signalling the structure of a lesson with headings. The goal is not to simplify the subject itself, but to remove obstacles that prevent the learner from focusing on what the subject actually requires them to think about.

We are going to look today at the relationship between urban living and infectious disease in the pre-industrial world. Early cities were dense, insanitary, and dependent on water sources that often lay downstream of waste disposal. Under those conditions, faecal-oral pathogens such as typhoid and dysentery flourished, and respiratory infections like measles spread easily through crowded interiors. The historian William McNeill argued that these disease regimes helped decide which populations could sustain large urban centres and which could not. His argument has two parts. First, sustained urbanisation requires either cultural practices that limit contamination, such as careful handling of food and water, or biological resistance acquired through repeated exposure. Second, when two populations with different disease histories met, the result was often catastrophic. Eurasian populations carried a long roster of childhood diseases to which they had partial immunity. When they reached the Americas, those pathogens spread through communities that had never experienced them, with devastating effects. The pattern reminds us that the growth of cities is inseparable from the biology of the people who live in them.

Our final topic is the link between glacial retreat and sea level rise, which students often misunderstand. The most common error is to imagine that melting sea ice, such as the ice floating around Antarctica, raises sea levels directly.
In fact, floating ice already displaces its own weight in water, so its melting adds little to ocean volume.

The contribution to sea level rise comes mostly from land-based ice, including the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets and mountain glaciers. There are two main mechanisms. The first is surface meltwater, which flows to the ocean through rivers and subglacial channels. The second is the calving of icebergs from glacier termini that extend into the sea. Calving is sensitive to ocean temperature, because warmer water can undercut the leading edge of a glacier and accelerate its break-up. Recent observations suggest that calving now contributes a growing share of mass loss in regions like West Antarctica. The time scales also differ. Surface melt responds within years to changes in air temperature, while the dynamic response of an ice sheet can unfold over centuries, which is why long-term sea level projections remain uncertain.
c2: Student: Hi, I work at the campus library.
I wanted to ask about a book I put on hold earlier this week.

Librarian: Sure, I can help with that. Do you have your student ID?
Student: Yes, here you go. The book is called Introduction to Marine Biology, and I think the hold was placed on Monday.
Librarian: Let me check our system. Yes, I see the request. Right now the book is still checked out to another student, and it is due back on Friday.
Student: So it will be available this weekend?
Librarian: Most likely. When it is returned, we will hold it at the front desk for forty eight hours. You will get an email when it is ready.
Student: Perfect. One more question, can I renew the book once I pick it up, or is that only for original borrowers?
Librarian: Students on the hold list can also renew, as long as no one else is waiting. You can do it online or at the desk.
Student: Great, thank you for explaining that.
Librarian: You are welcome. Have a good day.

Male student: Hey, are you free to talk about the group project for our environmental science class?
Female student: Sure, I have a few minutes before my next lecture. What do you need to discuss?
Male student: We need to pick a case study. I was thinking about focusing on water pollution in coastal cities. What do you think?
Female student: That sounds good, but two other groups already chose that topic. Our professor suggested picking something less common.
Male student: Right, I forgot about that. How about urban air quality? We could compare two cities with different policies.
Female student: I like that better. I can gather data on the first city if you handle the second one. When do we want to meet to write the report together?
Male student:
Could we meet on Thursday afternoon in the study room on the third floor?

Female student: Thursday works for me. I will bring my laptop and notes.
Male student: Great, I will reserve the room and send everyone a confirmation email.

Student: Professor Chen, do you have a moment? I am worried about the lab report I submitted yesterday.
Professor: Of course, come in. What is the issue?
Student:
I think I may have attached the wrong file.

The document I sent was an older draft, not the final version with the corrected data table.
Professor: I see. I have not opened the attachment yet because I usually review all reports over the weekend.
Student: Is there any way I can send you the correct file before you grade it?
Professor: Yes, please email it to me by Friday evening, and mention the original submission in the message so I can match them. I will replace the file in my folder.
Student: Thank you. I will send it right after this meeting.
Professor: No problem. For next time, consider including your name and the date in the file name to avoid confusion.
Student: That is a good idea. Thanks again, Professor.

Student: Hello, this is Maya from the campus bookstore. I am calling about my work schedule for next week.
Manager: Hi Maya, I have it right here. You are currently scheduled for Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday.
Student: I just realized there is a required workshop for my major on Saturday morning.
Is there any way I can swap that shift with a coworker?

Manager: Let me think. Daniel usually wants extra hours, so he might be willing to cover. I will send him a message and let you know by tomorrow.
Student: That would be great. If Daniel can take it, do I still need to do anything?
Manager: Yes, please confirm the swap with him directly, and then I will update the schedule so payroll is correct.
Student: Sounds good. Thanks for being flexible.
Manager: No problem. I will email you once I hear back from Daniel.
a2: Good morning, students. This is a brief announcement from the main campus library.
Beginning next Monday, the library will extend its weekday opening hours to better support evening study.

The new schedule will be Monday through Thursday from 7:30 a.m. to 11:00 p.m., and on Friday from 7:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Weekend hours remain unchanged: Saturday from 9:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., and Sunday from 10:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. The third floor quiet study zone will close fifteen minutes before the building closes, so please plan to gather your belongings in advance. Group study rooms on the second floor can still be booked through the library website up to one week in advance. We remind everyone that food is not allowed near the computer stations, but covered drinks are welcome. Thank you for your cooperation, and we wish you a productive week of study.
Attention, students. The campus dining services office would like to inform you about an update to the cafeteria payment system.
Starting tomorrow, the cashier stations will accept only the new student ID card and the official campus payment app.

Old magnetic stripe cards will no longer be accepted, and cash payments will be limited to a small number of designated registers near the south entrance. If you have not yet linked your student account to the campus payment app, please visit the dining services desk before the end of the week. Volunteers will be available today and tomorrow between noon and 3:00 p.m. to help with the setup process. The mobile app allows you to check your balance, view the daily menu, and add funds using a debit or credit card. Thank you for your patience during this transition.
Hello, this is the transportation office with a quick update about the campus shuttle service.
Due to construction near the engineering building, the Blue Line shuttle will follow a temporary route for the next three weeks.

The revised route will stop at the science library, the student center, the north parking lot, and the residence hall, but it will skip the engineering building stop. A replacement shuttle, called the Engineering Express, will run every fifteen minutes between the main gate and the engineering building during peak hours. Peak hours are defined as 8:00 to 10:00 in the morning and 4:00 to 6:00 in the afternoon. Outside of those times, students are encouraged to use the standard Blue Line service. The Green Line and the Red Line routes are not affected. Please check the transportation website for the updated map.
Good afternoon, everyone. The career development center would like to remind all students about the upcoming fall career fair.
The event will take place this Thursday from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. in the main gymnasium.

More than forty companies are expected to attend, including firms in engineering, business, information technology, and the nonprofit sector. Students are encouraged to bring several printed copies of their resume and to dress in business casual attire. Before the fair, the career center will host two preparation workshops: one on resume writing tomorrow at 2:00 p.m., and one on interview skills on Wednesday at 3:00 p.m. Both workshops will be held in room 210 of the student center. Online registration is available through the career center website, but walk in participants are also welcome. We look forward to seeing you there.
